beats: Hook: copy and paste is the most basic operation in computing (line_qc_cnot_stamp_rows); here is a three-line proof that no quantum gate can ever do it. Same cast: the tinkerer and the skeptic.

Why two-qubit gates matter: one-qubit gates keep separate qubits separate; two-qubit gates create entanglement, and on hardware they are the slow, noisy ones (Q24-05 01:25-05:43; Q25-05 57:02-58:28; line_qc_cnot_three_legged: two runners tied together are clumsier than either alone).
CNOT is a controlled XOR, (z1, z2) -> (z1, z1 xor z2): flip the target if the control is 1 (Q25-06 01:44-05:52; Q24-05 06:15-12:40; line_qc_cnot_flip_card).

H then CNOT makes the Bell pair (|00> + |11>)/sqrt2; entanglement is a critical computational resource (Q25-05 61:47-66:34; Q25-06 06:05-08:22, clip 07:26-08:22; line_qc_cnot_twin_dice, reuse line_dice_hand). Caveat captions with the dice: each die alone is a fair random roll and nobody can choose the shared result, so no message travels; the dice picture the agreement, not the mechanism (QC04-04 shows the quantum version beats any pre-agreed trick).

The "if and else at once" intuition (clip 63:07-63:56) only with the honest caption from Q24-02 p32: measuring returns one branch, at random (reuse line_spec_play_or_study or line_two_lanterns). Never caption it as "computes all answers at once".
Two CNOTs undo the entanglement: CNOT is its own inverse (Q24-05 20:47-21:38, her answer only; code; reuse line_qc_undo_twist_cube).

Fan-out is not a copy: CNOT onto a |0> gives alpha|00> + beta|11>, two qubits that always agree when read in the Z basis, not two independent copies of alpha|0> + beta|1>; a reflection moves with you but you cannot take it away and use it on its own (Q25-05 67:02-70:55; Q25-06 14:44-17:34; line_qc_cnot_mirror). Fan-out is used in distributed quantum computing.

No-cloning in three lines: if one U copied both |psi> and |phi>, unitarity gives <psi|phi> = <psi|phi>^2, so the two must be identical or orthogonal; known, distinguishable cards copy fine, an unknown sealed state cannot (Q25-06 08:29-14:44, clip 13:36-14:32 "you cannot really have a general copying machine in quantum computing"; Wootters & Zurek 1982, Dieks 1982; line_qc_cnot_copier_envelope).
Cover (line_cover_qc05_04; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): the tinkerer offers a sealed envelope to an old photocopier; the skeptic, arms crossed, shakes their head.
